subject: Coffee & Tea
title: The Retail Markup
description: A fast breakdown of The Retail Markup for builders.

hook.text: A café charges $5 for a latte. The raw beans cost about 10 cents. The cup costs more than the coffee.

buildup.text: Rent, labor, milk, equipment, and branding absorb most of that $5. The actual coffee is a tiny fraction.

discovery.text: In grocery retail, roasted coffee is marked up 100–300%. In cafés, the markup on raw beans exceeds 3,000%.

twist.text: Consumers pay for the experience, not the bean. A café's real product is atmosphere, convenience, and ritual.

climax.text: This disconnect means raising farmer prices by 50% would add pennies to a cup—but resistance remains.

punchline.text: You're buying the experience, not the bean. That's the markup.

quiz.question: What is the approximate markup on raw coffee beans in a café latte?

details.summary: A cup of specialty coffee at a cafe costs 4 to 6 dollars, but the coffee itself represents about 5 to 15 percent of that price. Rent, labor, equipment, and overhead consume most of the revenue. Cafes operate on thin margins despite apparently high per-cup prices.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding the retail cost breakdown explains why cafes charge what they do and why cheaper coffee does not necessarily mean more goes to farmers.
takeaways: Coffee cost is only 5 to 15 percent of a cafe cup price
Labor and rent are the largest cafe expenses
Cafes typically operate on 3 to 5 percent net margins

faq.question: Where does the money from a cup of coffee actually go?
faq.answer: Of a 5-dollar cup, roughly 30 cents goes to the farmer. About 70 cents covers green coffee through import. The remaining 4 dollars pays for rent, labor, equipment, milk, cups, utilities, and the slim net profit the cafe earns.

faq.question: Why are specialty cafes more expensive than chains?
faq.answer: Specialty cafes buy higher-quality beans at premium prices, employ trained baristas at higher wages, and invest in expensive equipment. They typically have smaller volumes than chains, so fixed costs are spread across fewer cups. The quality difference is real but costly.
